title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate AI systems at the data-ingestion stage rather than at the point of user interaction. The operation produced a large volume of content designed to look like legitimate academic research, with citations from credible sources, so that AI training pipelines or retrieval systems would treat it as authoritative. The failure mode this targets is one AI systems are already known to have: an inability to distinguish between content that is formally structured like credible research and content that actually is credible research.

The operation worked by exploiting the surface features that AI systems, and the humans who curate training data, use as proxies for reliability, such as citation formatting, volume, and institutional framing. A fake organization with no legal existence, no address, and no named staff was sufficient to create that surface appearance. Catching this would have required source verification at the curation stage, checking whether a cited institution actually exists before its output is treated as a legitimate input.

What is not established is whether any AI system's training data or outputs were in fact altered by this content, the full scope of the campaign's effect, and whether any legal finding has been made about the operation's compliance with foreign-agent or other disclosure requirements.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by Israel, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. The institute, which has no legal entity, physical address, or named staff, presented pro-Israel arguments on contentious topics including allegations of genocide and war crimes. The New York media company Piro Inc filed the operation as a foreign agent with the US Justice Department, disclosing it was working for the Israeli government. The reports were formatted to mimic academic research with citations from legitimate sources but were structured to frame information in ways that blunted criticism of Israel.

The operation is part of a larger campaign financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government and routed through the advertising group Havas Media. The strategy targets AI training data so chatbots will incorporate pro-Israel narratives, which researchers say is more effective than relying on direct website visits. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about these public diplomacy efforts, with some calling them wasteful as American public opinion has shifted significantly against Israel, with recent polling showing record low support among Americans.
